cards.explanation: The day that is near is the Day of the LORD. The verse says it plainly: "…the Day of the LORD is near." Then it describes that day as "…a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Right before that, God tells Ezekiel to say, "Wail, ‘Alas for that day!’" (Ezekiel 30:2)
The answer is False. The verse says the day "…will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations." Doom is the opposite of peace, friends. So the verse says doom, not peace.
The word is anguish. The verse says "…there will be anguish in Cush when the slain fall in Egypt…" Cush is Egypt's neighbor to the south. Anguish is the word God gives for Cush in that moment.
The word is collapse, friends. God says, "…her proud strength will collapse." The verse puts that right alongside the fall of Egypt's allies. Picture a tall stack of cookie boxes coming down.

The answer is that they will know He is the LORD. God says, "Then they will know that I am the LORD…" when He sets fire to Egypt and her helpers are shattered. That line comes back again and again in this chapter, bakers.

The answer is to frighten Cush out of complacency. The verse says God's messengers go out in ships "…to frighten Cush out of complacency." Complacency means feeling too settled to worry. Those ships are headed straight for Cush, and I think it's going to be a wake-up call.

The answer is True, friends. God says, "He and his people with him, the most ruthless of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land." Nebuchadnezzar is the king of Babylon. When God uses that kind of description, it tells you what Egypt is facing.

God says He will make the streams dry up. His words are, "I will make the streams dry up…" Streams are what keep a land going, so this is a serious thing to say, bakers. It's one more way God shows He isn't done.

The word is foreigners. God says, "By the hands of foreigners I will bring desolation upon the land and everything in it." Right before that, He says He will sell the land to the wicked. Then He ends with "I, the LORD, have spoken."
The answer is False, friends. God says, "There will no longer be a prince in Egypt, and I will instill fear in that land." The land is losing its prince. It's not a small thing.
The word is fear. God says, "…I will instill fear in that land." It comes right after He says there will no longer be a prince in Egypt, bakers. The word is fear, and the verse stays with it.
The word is cloud, friends. God says, "A cloud will cover her…" It comes right after the day is darkened in Tahpanhes. The cloud echoes the "…day of clouds…" from the start of the chapter.

The answer is his arm. God says, "…I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt." He adds that it "…has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword." So it's Pharaoh's arm, bakers.

God says He will break the strong arm and the broken one. His words are, "I will break his arms, both the strong one and the one already broken…" That means both are going, friends. After that, the sword falls from his hand.

The word is sword. God says He "…will make the sword fall from his hand." It ties back to the arm that had not been splinted "…for strength to hold the sword." Without strong arms, that sword isn't staying in his hand, bakers.

The answer is True, friends. God says, "I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king and place My sword in his hand…" So while Pharaoh's arms are breaking, the king of Babylon's arms are getting stronger. Two kings, two very different directions.
The answer is True, bakers. God says He will break the arms of Pharaoh, "…who will groan before him like a mortally wounded man." I think this one is a heavy picture.
